title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Runbooks
author: Asha Patel
body:
Overview:

This document consolidates the canonical reference for the Redwood Inference serving runtime: architecture, kernel selection & scheduling policy, profiling/playbooks, benchmarking suite, release notes, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended for engineers on serving-runtime, eng-sre, and platform teams who operate or modify inference components.

Goals:
- Describe the high-level architecture and data flows for the runtime.
- Formalize kernel selection and scheduling policies that balance latency, throughput and cost.
- Provide a step-by-step profiling/playbook for performance regressions.
- Outline the benchmarking suite and standard scenarios used for capacity planning.
- Capture recent release notes and current known issues.
- Provide runbooks for common incidents and links to the team wiki.

1) System architecture (summary)

High-level services:
- runtime-controller: orchestration, model version routing, rollouts and health checks.
- inference-worker: per-GPU worker running the compiled model kernel and handling KV cache.
- batcher: request coalescing service responsible for composing micro-batches into GPU batches.
- kernel-selector: selects execution kernels (FP32/FP16/INT8 kernels and custom attention kernels) based on model profile and request metadata.
- kv-cache-service: shared prefix/KV cache for warm prompt reuse (TTL + LRU heuristics).
- tracer: distributed tracing collector (Jaeger-compatible) and token-level timeline exporter.

Data flow (short): inbound API -> runtime-controller -> routing -> batcher -> inference-worker -> kernel -> kv-cache lookup/commit -> response streaming.

SLOs and operational thresholds:
- Availability: 99.95% (per-region)
- Latency (text-generation): p50 < 120ms, p95 < 300ms for short prompts (<128 tokens) on hosted tier; p95 SLO for dedicated capacity depends on reserved profile but targeted <200ms.
- Token throughput (per GPU): baseline depends on model; example: 70 tokens/s for rw-7b-quant across A100-80GB when using the fused-attention kernel.
- Error budget: 0.05% request errors monthly.

Ownership:
- runtime-controller, kernel-selector: runtime-team (service owners: @miguel, @asha)
- inference-worker, batcher: serving-engine-team (owners: @ravi)
- kv-cache-service: infra-cache team (owner: @elena)

2) Kernel scheduling and selection policy

Objectives: maximize tail-latency headroom and GPU utilization while respecting per-request latency constraints and customer routing policies.

Policy overview (priority order):
1. Hard latency deadline: if request annotated with max_latency_ms, we prefer lower-latency kernels or single-request scheduling.
2. Model compatibility and quantization profile: kernel-selector filters kernels that support the model architecture, sequence length, and quantization (INT8/FP16).
3. Throughput optimization: when latency budget allows, group small requests into batching windows (default batch_window_ms = 8ms).
4. Graceful fallback: on kernel failure or slow path, fallback to compatibility kernels with safety guard rails and adaptive batching.

Key knobs and defaults (config table):
| parameter | default | description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| batch_window_ms | 8 | Maximum coalescing window before issuing a GPU batch |
| max_batch_size | 128 | Hard per-GPU batch size ceiling |
| tail_latency_mode | adaptive | 'adaptive'|'conservative'|'aggressive' kernel selection strategy |
| kv_cache_ttl_s | 300 | TTL for KV cache entries (seconds) |
| pref_kernels | [fused_attention, fast_gemm] | Kernel preference order for new models |

Kernel selection examples (pseudocode):
```python
def choose_kernel(model_profile, request):
    candidates = kernel_catalog.filter(arch=model_profile.arch, seq_len=request.seq_len)
    if request.max_latency_ms is not None:
        candidates = candidates.sort_by(estimated_p95_latency)
    if model_profile.quant == 'int8':
        candidates = candidates.filter(supports_int8=True)
    return candidates[0]  # top preference after policy scoring
```

Scheduling modes:
- single-shot: one request per GPU (used for strict latency-critical requests).
- batching: micro-batching window + dynamic batch sizing (default).
- pooled: long-running streams where tokens are appended to an open batch and served every N ms.

3) Profiling playbook (step-by-step)

When a performance regression is detected (alerts: p95 latency spike > 25% baseline or available GPU throughput drop > 20%), follow this playbook: 

1. Triage & scope
   - Identify affected service(s) via dashboards: runtime-controller, batcher, inference-worker.
   - Determine scope: model(s) impacted, regions, customer tier.
   - Gather traces for a representative time window (use tracer UI and token-level timeline).

2. Hypothesis checklist
   - Kernel regression: new kernel rollout or updated kernel flags? Check kernel-selector versions.
   - Batch size distribution shift: run distribution summary for last 1h.
   - KV cache churn: elevated cache miss rate -> increased compute.
   - Hardware/driver changes: driver (NVIDIA) or CUDA upgrade events.
   - Noisy neighbor/backpressure from other pods: check cgroup/GPU metrics.

3. Profiling commands and artifacts
   - Capture GPU timeline (nsight or CUPTI wrapper): /opt/tools/gpu-timeline --pid <worker-pid> --out /tmp/tl.gz
   - Export inference-worker metrics: curl -s http://inference-worker:9100/metrics > metrics.json
   - Sample process stack: gdb --pid <pid> --batch -ex "thread apply all bt" > stacks.txt

4. Quick mitigations
   - Rollback kernel selector to previous stable version: runtime-controller rollout revert <kernel-selector> --to-revision vX.Y.Z
   - Force single-shot scheduling for affected customers: runtime-controller update-route --route-id <route> --scheduling single-shot
   - Increase batch_window_ms temporarily to reduce scheduling pressure: curl -X PATCH ... (see config snippet below).

5. Root cause and follow-up
   - Open a postmortem if impact crosses severity level P1/P2 (see oncall incident process).
   - If kernel bug, create a tracking ticket in internal tracker and assign to kernel owners.

4) Benchmarking suite and standard scenarios

The benchmarking harness lives in infra/benchmarks/serving-runtime. Benchmarks are reproducible and tagged by model, hardware, and kernel config. Core scenarios:
- short-chat: prompt length 16 tokens, generation length 64, 50 concurrent clients, measure p50/p95 latency and tokens/sec.
- long-dialogue: prefix 1024 tokens, generation length 128, streaming response, measure KV cache hit-rate and incremental latency.
- embed-bulk: batched embedding compute 1000 inputs, measure throughput and GPU mem pressure.

Standard benchmark metadata (JSON):
```json
{
  "model": "rw-7b",
  "hardware": "a100-80gb",
  "kernel_profile": "fused_attention_fp16",
  "concurrency": 50,
  "run_id": "2026-03-01-short-chat"
}
```

How to run (example):
```bash
# from infra/benchmarks/serving-runtime
./run_bench.sh --model rw-7b --hardware a100-80gb --scenario short-chat --out results/short-chat-$(date +%F).json
```

Benchmark acceptance criteria for new kernel changes:
- p95 latency regression <= 10% vs baseline for short-chat 
- token throughput change <= 5% vs baseline for long runs (>=30m)
- mem usage increase <= 8%

5) Release notes (recent entries)

2026-03-08 - v3.4.1 (runtime-controller + kernel-selector)
- Fixed race in kernel-selector that could cause stale kernel rankings after topology changes.
- Improved scoring to prefer fused-attention for sequence lengths <= 512.
- Rollout: canary 5% -> 25% -> 100% over 72h.

2026-02-10 - v3.3.0 (inference-worker)
- Added CUPTI-based sampling for token-level profiler.
- Default batch_window_ms reduced from 10ms -> 8ms to improve p50 for microburst traffic.

6) Known issues (current)

- ISSUE-2026-ALPHA: Intermittent increased p95 latency for rw-13b-quant on A100 following CUDA 12.2 driver update. Workaround: pin driver to 525.x until patch. (owner: infra-team)
- ISSUE-2025-KV-CHURN: High KV cache churn for multi-tenant workloads with highly variable prefixes. Mitigation: per-tenant cache partitioning, increase kv_cache_ttl_s to 600 for heavy chat customers.
- ISSUE-2026-BATCH-EDGE: When batch_window_ms is set <4ms, micro-batch sampling can cause starvation under bursty traffic. Avoid <4ms unless single-shot mode is used.

7) Runtime runbooks (incident playbooks)

P1: Large-scale latency/throughput regression (affects multiple customers/regions)
1. Pager alert -> oncall SRE joins incident channel.
2. Triage: check control-plane for recent rollouts (runtime-controller).
3. Run quick mitigations: reduce canary traffic, rollback kernel-selector, force single-shot for top-10 affected routes.
4. Collect artifacts (traces, metrics, GPU timelines).
5. Engage kernel and infra-driver owners; escalate to platform manager if rollback fails.

P2: Single-model severe degradation (one model shows 5x p95 increase)
1. Isolate: move requests for that model to a dedicated inference-pool.
2. Reduce concurrency to lower memory pressure: route-level throttle.
3. Profile: use token-level tracer and CUPTI timelines.

Operational commands (examples):
- runtime-controller rollout status --service kernel-selector --region us-west1
- runtime-controller update-config --component batcher --set batch_window_ms=12
- kubectl -n serving get pods -l app=inference-worker -o wide

Appendix A — Config examples

runtime-controller config (YAML snippet):
```yaml
runtime_controller:
  scheduling:
    default_batch_window_ms: 8
    max_batch_size: 128
    tail_latency_mode: adaptive
  kernel_selector:
    preferred: ["fused_attention_fp16","fast_gemm_fp16"]
    fallback: ["compat_gemm_fp32"]
```

Kernel-selector scoring sample (JSON):
```json
{"kernel":"fused_attention_fp16","estimated_p95_ms":180,"mem_bytes":32000000000}
```
